title: The linked groups
question: Which flagged organizations, firms, people and addresses hang together, and which groups hold the most independent warning signs?
finding: 111 linked groups were found among 2,305 flagged organizations, firms and addresses. The top-ranked group is named after Felton Institute: 6 members carrying 46 different kinds of warning sign and $426.9 million of City money since fiscal 2019; of its members none is a party to a proven or charged case, one is the subject of an official finding of its own, and 3 are named in the file of a proven or charged case without being a party; attached to it by one route: Gwendolyn Westbrook, party to a charged case (charged; not decided, 2026-02-23). Across all 111 groups, 4 hold a member that is itself a party to a proven or charged case, 19 hold a member that is the subject of an official finding, and 4 hold a member that is only named in such a case file.
how: A graph was built from the relationships the other screens already hold. Nodes: organizations and firms (names normalised; two spellings of one name are merged), San Francisco street addresses, and people who are officers on a tax return, registered lobbyists or permit consultants, or officials. Links, each tagged with its kind and source: shares an officer; same address; pays (grant, largest-contractor payment or rent); lobbies or consults for; gives to the campaign of; gift to an official; payment at an official's request; official's seat, income or investment; staff who moved; shares a State-licensed person; drawn together in a case file. Removed first, by rule: the City and public bodies, banks, utilities, title, payroll and insurance firms, law and accounting firms, universities and hospitals (by name); any node's links of one kind when that kind ties it to more than 12 others; any address with 25 or more active business registrations, kept only where two parties share a suite with fewer than 8; and addresses the assessor classes as houses, condominiums or small flats, which are never listed. A person appears only when the name is on file in a public role (officer or director on a tax return, Form 700 filer, candidate or office-holder, registered lobbyist or permit consultant, City employee, or party in a case record), only on a full name that is rare (the test in the people screen), and only where each tie has a second, independent record: for a name on a tax return, the two organizations it would join are themselves tied in another way (money, an address, a case file, or two shared names) or the person's own City department pays the organization; for any other tie, a public-role record from a different source than the one reporting the tie. Every person shown is a name match, not a confirmed identity. Nodes with no warning sign that hang by one link were dropped. A member's own standing is kept apart from the case files it is named in: it is a party only if the record of case outcomes lists it as one (proven if convicted, pleaded, admitted or stipulated; charged if charged and not decided; none if dismissed or settled without admission); it is the subject of an official finding only if an audit, monitoring finding, suspension or debarment, regulator's status or penalty names it; being named in a case file is a third thing and carries no standing. Groups are the connected sets that remain; a set of more than 40 members is replaced by its cores, where every link is backed by a second kind of link between the same two members or by a third member tied to both. Members hanging off one core by a single route are listed as attached but not counted. Ranked by the number of different kinds of warning sign the members carry (as recorded in the flag map), then by the number of members that are a party to a case or the subject of an official finding, then by City payments in fiscal 2019 to 2026. Each group is named after the member the City paid most.
limits: Being linked is not being involved: nonprofits share board members, buildings and auditors all the time, and San Francisco is a small city. A group is a place to look, ranked by how many independent signs sit inside it. An organization named in the file of a charged case is not charged: some are fiscal sponsors or grantees that reported the problem or were its victims, which is why parties, subjects of findings and organizations only named in a file are counted in three separate columns. A larger group collects more kinds of sign simply by being larger, and several signs come from the same tax returns, so they are not fully independent. The same firm under two different names stays two members; subsidiaries are not joined to parents unless a record ties them. Where another screen publishes only its first rows (foundation board overlaps, permit-consultant clients, lobbyists who gave), only those rows are in the graph, so links are missing rather than invented. Shares an officer or director (name match): board members often serve several organizations, and affiliates share leaders as a matter of course. Same street address: nonprofit centres, landlords and tenants, and fiscal sponsors share buildings. Pays (grant, contract or rent): sub-grants and specialist contractors are how programmes are delivered. Gives to the campaign of: campaign donations are reported, with limits on amounts. Payment at an official's request: officials must disclose charitable payments they ask for. Drawn together in a case file: a case file also names bystanders, victims and people who were cleared.
